records.title: Preoperative depressive symptoms as an independent prognostic factor for long-term survival after curative-intent treatment for hepatocellular carcinoma: a prospective cohort study
records.abstract: BACKGROUND: Depression is common in cancer patients and may affect prognosis, yet its impact on long-term outcomes after curative-intent treatment for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is underexplored. We prospectively examined whether preoperative depressive symptoms (Zung Self-Rating Depression Scale score ≥ 53) independently predict poorer overall survival (OS) and disease-free survival (DFS) in HCC patients undergoing curative-intent treatment. METHODS: A total of 213 pathologically confirmed HCC patients who underwent resection or ablation at Xiangya Hospital (2019) were enrolled. Depressive status was assessed by the Zung Self-Rating Depression Scale (cutoff≥53), dividing patients into screen-positive (n = 66) and screen-negative (n = 147) groups. The primary endpoint was OS; the secondary endpoint was DFS. Follow-up ended December 2025. Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression analyses adjusted for demographic, clinical, pathological, and treatment covariates. RESULTS: The screen-positive group included more females (21.2% vs. 10.9%, P = 0.05) and more patients with low educational attainment (69.7% vs. 52.4%, P = 0.04), whereas partner status and alcohol use were balanced. Median follow-up was 77 months. Depressive symptoms significantly worsened DFS (median 12.0 vs. 24.0 months; HR = 1.42, P = 0.02) and OS (median 41.0 vs. 55.0 months; HR = 1.78, P < 0.001). Multivariable Cox analysis confirmed depressive symptoms as an independent adverse factor for both DFS (HR = 1.45, 95% CI: 1.04-2.01, P = 0.03) and OS (HR = 1.50, 95% CI: 1.05-2.14, P = 0.03). The DFS model adjusted for age, partner status, BCLC stage, AFP, type of surgery, MVI, and Ki-67; the OS model additionally adjusted for educational attainment and alcohol use status. CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative depressive symptoms independently predict shorter DFS and OS after curative-intent treatment for HCC. Routine screening for depressive symptoms may help identify patients at higher risk; whether psychosocial intervention improves long-term outcomes requires further study.

records.title: Very Early Recurrence as a Dynamic Prognostic Stratifier After Curative Hepatectomy for Hepatocellular Carcinoma: A Landmark Analysis with Internal Validation and Machine-Learning Benchmarking
records.abstract: Background: Very early recurrence (VER, defined as recurrence within 12 months) after hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) resection is often linked to poor survival, but conventional survival analyses stratified by recurrence status are inherently susceptible to guarantee-time bias. The relation between VER and post-recurrence survival also remains uncertain. Methods: This retrospective cohort included 526 patients with histopathologically confirmed HCC who underwent curative hepatectomy at the First Affiliated Hospital of Xinjiang Medical University between January 2016 and July 2025. A 12-month landmark cohort included patients alive beyond 12 months after surgery. Patients were split 7:3 into training and internally held-out validation cohorts. Landmark Cox models, a time-varying Cox model, post-recurrence survival analyses, and machine-learning benchmarking were performed. Missing primary-model values were median-imputed; multiple imputation was not used. Results: The landmark cohort included 486 patients; 82 had VER. The proportional-hazards assumption was violated for VER; the conventional adjusted Cox model estimated an average HR of 3.86 (95% CI, 2.81-5.29; P < 0.001) over post-landmark follow-up. The association varied over time, with model-estimated HRs of 10.06 at 1 month and 2.23 at 60 months after the landmark. In the internally held-out validation cohort, adding VER to the conventional Cox model improved the C-index from 0.591 (95% CI, 0.508-0.675) to 0.716 (95% CI, 0.633-0.797; C-index difference = 0.125, 95% CI, 0.051-0.203; P = 0.002). VER was not independently associated with post-recurrence mortality (HR, 1.23; 95% CI, 0.87-1.75; P = 0.25). Conclusions: Among patients alive at the 12-month landmark, VER was associated with higher subsequent mortality and improved discrimination in an internally held-out cohort. External validation is required before use for individual risk prediction or surveillance decisions.

records.title: Spatial Immune Remodeling during Neoadjuvant Therapy in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: Mechanisms, Clinical Implications, and Future Perspectives
records.abstract: : Neoadjuvant therapy is an emerging strategy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), particularly in cases with technically resectable but biologically high-risk disease. Neoadjuvant therapy aims to reduce tumor burden and postoperative recurrence risk in high-risk HCC, while also providing a unique opportunity to preoperatively remodel the tumor microenvironment (TME). Recent advances in spatial multiomics have shown that the HCC immune microenvironment is highly heterogeneous, with distinct immune landscapes across the tumor core, invasive front, and adjacent liver tissue. At the spatial level, neoadjuvant therapy may reorganize the HCC tumor microenvironment beyond simple changes in immune-cell abundance. It reshapes the localization and interaction networks of tumor, immune, stromal, and vascular cells, including immune-cell infiltration into tumor nests, tumor–immune cell proximity, vascular accessibility, fibrotic exclusion barriers, and residual resistant niches. Collectively, these spatial changes influence pathological response, microvascular invasion, recurrence risk, and perioperative decision-making. However, key challenges include optimal patient selection, response evaluation, treatment sequencing, surgery timing, and perioperative safety management. Future integration of spatial omics, ctDNA, radiomics, digital pathology, and artificial intelligence may enable further developments in biology-guided neoadjuvant therapy and precise perioperative management of HCC.

records.title: Serum Protein Panel Facilitates Surgical Decision-Making for Barcelona Stage B Hepatocellular Carcinoma
records.abstract: PURPOSE: To develop a serum proteomic-based prognostic model for predicting surgical outcomes in BCLC stage B hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) patients, addressing the clinical heterogeneity that limits uniform treatment recommendations. METHODS: Preoperative serum samples from HCC patients undergoing curative resection were retrospectively collected and subjected to proteomic profiling using nanoparticle-enhanced data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry (DIA-MS). A prognostic risk model was developed in a training cohort (N = 52, BCLC stage B) using 5-fold cross-validated Lasso-Cox machine learning, with overall survival (OS) as the primary endpoint. The model was validated in an independent BCLC stage B cohort (N = 22), extended to a single huge HCC cohort (N = 26, BCLC stage A HCC with a solitary tumor measuring at least 10 cm), and benchmarked against a comparison cohort (N = 190, BCLC 0/A without huge HCC). Orthogonal validation was performed by parallel reaction monitoring (PRM) in an exploration cohort (N = 51, BCLC stage B HCC). RESULTS: Among 2,381 identified proteins, a three-protein panel (LCP1, DOK3, CNN2) was selected to construct the model. The model demonstrated strong predictive accuracy for 3-year OS in the training cohort (AUC = 0.936, sensitivity = 0.988, specificity = 0.834), outperforming the clinical Kinki criteria, in the validation cohort (AUC = 0.812, sensitivity = 0.875, specificity = 0.786) and in the extended cohort of huge HCC patients (AUC = 0.758, sensitivity = 0.709, specificity = 0.852). Notably, low-risk BCLC stage B patients showed comparable prognosis to the comparison cohort of BCLC 0/A patients, suggesting potential surgical benefit. The PRM validation in an independent exploration cohort confirmed the model's prognostic value (AUC = 0.800, sensitivity = 0.870, specificity = 0.700). CONCLUSIONS: This serum proteomic-based prognostic model accurately predicts surgical outcomes for BCLC stage B HCC patients and outperforms clinical stratification. By identifying low-risk patients who may benefit from surgery, this tool facilitates personalized treatment planning and has the potential to improve survival and quality of life.

records.title: Machine Learning Model Integrating Conventional Ultrasound Radiomics and Clinicopathological Features for Early Recurrence Risk Prediction After Curative-Intent Hepatectomy in Hepatocellular Carcinoma
records.abstract: Purpose: To develop and compare machine learning models integrating conventional ultrasound radiomic features with clinicopathological variables for predicting one-year postoperative recurrence in patients with hepatocellular carcinoma after curative-intent hepatectomy. Methods: This retrospective, single-center study included 154 patients with pathologically confirmed hepatocellular carcinoma who underwent curative-intent hepatectomy between January 2020 and December 2024. Patients were divided into a training cohort (n = 124) and a validation cohort (n = 30). Clinicopathological data and preoperative conventional ultrasound images were collected. Radiomic features were extracted and selected using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. Predictive models were developed and compared using conventional logistic regression and four machine learning algorithms, including a generalized linear model (GLM), random forest (RF), support vector machine (SVM), and gradient boosting machine (GBM), based on different combinations of clinicopathological variables and radiomic features. Model performance was evaluated in the validation cohort. Results: Multivariable logistic regression identified Edmondson grade, satellite nodules, fibrinogen, and white blood cell count as factors independently associated with postoperative recurrence. Among the evaluated models, the RF model combining clinicopathological factors with the Radscore achieved the highest numerical validation area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.717 (95% confidence interval: 0.523-0.910), with an accuracy of 70.0%, a sensitivity of 42.9%, and a specificity of 93.8%. Conclusion: The RF model integrating clinicopathological factors with the Radscore showed moderate discrimination for one-year postoperative recurrence and may hold promise for postoperative risk assessment. Given the limited validation sample size and uncertainty in model performance, these findings should be considered exploratory and require further validation in larger, independent, multicenter cohorts before clinical implementation.
